opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core challenge is that "messiness" is a really hard thing to pin down. When we talk about a task being messy, we're gesturing at a cluster of properties: maybe the task isn't well specified, maybe there's no clean feedback signal telling you whether you're on track, maybe you have to deal with a dynamic environment, or coordinate with other agents, or the resources you need aren't clearly laid out for you. Real-world work tends to have a lot of these properties, and benchmark tasks tend to have fewer of them, because they're constructed to be automatically scorable and reproducible.

So the intuitive story is that models do great on benchmarks but less well on real work because real work is messier. But when you try to actually test that, you run into a few problems.

One is measurement. You have to operationalize messiness somehow, usually by having people rate tasks on a set of factors, and those ratings are subjective and noisy. Different raters might disagree about how underspecified a task is, for example.

Another, and maybe the bigger one, is confounding. Messier tasks also tend to be longer, harder, and take humans more time. So if you see models doing worse on messier tasks, it's not obvious whether that's because of the messiness itself or just because those tasks are harder in a more generic sense. Disentangling those is tricky, especially when your dataset isn't huge and the tasks weren't designed to vary messiness independently of difficulty.

And then there's a selection issue: the tasks we can put in a benchmark at all are already filtered toward being less messy, because we need to be able to score them. So you don't really get to observe the full range of messiness you see in the real world. You're looking at a fairly restricted slice, which makes it hard to extrapolate. In our work we did see some signal that messier tasks were harder for models, but the trends in improvement over time looked fairly similar across messier and less messy subsets, so it's not like messiness is some wall that progress is stopping at. Still, I'd hold all of that with a fair amount of uncertainty given those challenges.

r001.rationale: The response says messiness is hard to pin down, describes it as a cluster of properties, and notes that raters may disagree about how underspecified a task is.

r002.rationale: The response mentions tasks that are not well specified, but does not distinguish carrying out a specified task from deciding what should be done.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main challenge is that "messiness" is really a bundle of a lot of different things, and we don't have a clean way to pull them apart. When we looked at the tasks in our benchmarks, we tried to come up with a bunch of factors that seemed like they'd make a task harder in ways that aren't captured by just, how long does it take a human to do this. Things like: is the task ambiguous, does it require interacting with a real environment where things can go wrong, is there a clear success criterion, does the person doing it need a lot of implicit context, is there some novel situation you have to adapt to. And when you score tasks along those dimensions, you do see that models tend to do worse on the messier ones, even controlling for how long the task takes a human.

But the problem is that those factors are correlated with each other, and they're also correlated with the thing we care about, which is how much a task resembles real work. So it's hard to say which of those is actually doing the work. Is it that models are bad at handling ambiguity specifically? Or is it that the messier tasks just happen to also be the ones that weren't designed with automated grading in mind, so we have less clean data about them? It's very easy to construct a story after the fact.

The other piece is that the ratings themselves are pretty subjective. We had people go through and rate tasks on these criteria, and reasonable people disagree about whether a given task is ambiguous or requires novel adaptation. So you've got noise in the measurement on top of the conceptual tangle. My honest take is that messiness is a useful pointer toward the gap between benchmarks and real work, but if you want it to be explanatory rather than descriptive, you probably need to deliberately construct tasks that vary one factor at a time, and that's expensive and hard to do well.

r001.rationale: The response says ratings are subjective and reasonable people disagree about whether tasks meet criteria such as ambiguity or novel adaptation, identifying this disagreement as a measurement problem.

r002.rationale: It mentions ambiguity and unclear success criteria, but does not distinguish executing a specified task from figuring out what should be done.

astra-6.text:
I think the main challenge is making “messiness” precise enough that it gives you a prediction, rather than a description after the fact. If a model does badly on a task, it’s tempting to say, well, that task is messy. But then what would have counted as evidence against the explanation?

There are also a bunch of different things that might get bundled together under messiness: ambiguous instructions, irrelevant information, having to interact with an environment, or having to do many steps without making a mistake. Those could be quite different difficulties for a model. So I’d want to separate those out and vary them while keeping the underlying task roughly fixed. Then we could ask which properties actually explain the change in performance, and whether that explanation carries over to other tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says “messiness” needs a precise definition and lists different properties it could include, but it does not identify disagreement over what counts as messy as a central obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response mentions ambiguous instructions and multi-step tasks, but does not distinguish carrying out a specified task from figuring out what should be done.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main challenge is defining messiness independently of how well the model does. It’s tempting to look at tasks where models struggle and say, “Well, those tasks are messy.” But then messiness isn’t really explaining the performance; it’s just redescribing it.

What you’d want is some way to characterize a task beforehand—how much relevant context is missing, whether the instructions are ambiguous, whether you need to interact with an environment—and then see whether those properties predict performance. And it’s difficult to separate those things from other explanations, like whether similar tasks appeared in training or how easy it is to check an answer. So I think it’s a plausible hypothesis, but turning it into a measurable, predictive explanation is the hard part.

r001.rationale: The response says messiness must be defined independently of performance, but does not identify disagreement over what counts as a messy task.

r002.rationale: It mentions ambiguous instructions and interaction with an environment, but does not distinguish carrying out a specified task from figuring out what should be done.
